text: Lnx-app-02 is Meridian Fabrication's internal application server, running the same shop-floor system that WIN-SRV-04 feeds data to. It's RHEL-based and about to join production, which means it gets the Linux side of the same checklist — the sudoers, SELinux, SSH, and auditing chapters, applied to one real box before go-live.

The existing sudoers file has a leftover wildcard entry letting the application service account run anything as root. That gets scoped down to exactly one command, restarting its own service, with no password prompt needed for that single case. Adding input and output logging to every sudo session means there's finally an answer to what an account actually ran.

SELinux on a freshly built box is often permissive, logging violations without blocking them, which isn't protecting anything yet. Flipping it the wrong way breaks the application, so the check comes first: search for existing denials, fix any mislabeled file contexts, then enforce. Making enforcing survive a reboot means editing the config file, not just the live setting.

SSH hardening and fail2ban are built to work together. No root login, no password fallback if a key goes missing, and a short list of users allowed to connect at all closes the door. Fail2ban then watches whoever keeps knocking, banning any address that trips four failed attempts within ten minutes for a full hour.

The last layer is auditd, pointed at exactly the files an auditor asks about: the password database, the shadow file, and sudoers itself. Persisted and loaded so they survive a reboot, these watch rules mean any write to one of those three files shows up in a search tagged privilege escalation, which is precisely what a real audit looks for.

Every one of those four steps closes a gap that, left open, becomes exactly the kind of finding an external audit flags. Next up, a case study walks through what happens when a company doesn't close those gaps first — a failed security audit, and the real remediation it takes to fix it.
